item.title: C++ Containers and Iterators
item.description:
Choose a container from the required lookup, traversal, insertion, erasure, memory locality, and reference-stability properties. Complexity describes an operation under its preconditions; invalidation and ownership determine whether a design remains correct after mutation.

Selecting a Container #

  • std::vector is the default sequence for contiguous storage, random access, cache locality, and C interoperation through data(). Appending is amortized constant time. Any capacity growth invalidates every iterator, pointer, and reference; without growth, insertion invalidates iterators and references at or after the insertion point.
  • std::deque supports indexed access. End insertion invalidates iterators but not references; its storage is non-contiguous, and middle insertion invalidates iterators and references.
  • std::list and std::forward_list retain iterators and references to unaffected nodes across insertion and erasure. Their node allocation and pointer chasing make them a measured choice, not a default.
  • std::map and std::set provide ordered traversal and logarithmic lookup. Insertion does not invalidate iterators or references, except erased elements.
  • std::unordered_map and std::unordered_set provide average constant-time lookup. Rehash invalidates iterators, although references and pointers to elements remain valid; erasing invalidates only the erased element.

reserve() avoids predicted vector reallocations and can also reduce unordered_* rehashing. It does not make an iterator valid after an operation whose documented rules invalidate it.

item.title: Clangd and Compilation Databases
item.description:
clangd provides C and C++ language-server features by parsing each open file with a virtual compiler command. Completion, diagnostics, navigation, and refactoring are reliable only when that command represents the real build context: working directory, compiler driver, target, language mode, include paths, preprocessor definitions, and generated headers.

item.title: SFINAE and Template Overload Resolution
item.description:
C++ substitutes template arguments while it forms function-template candidates. Substitution failure is not an error (SFINAE) means that an invalid dependent type or expression in the immediate context of that substitution removes that candidate; it does not make arbitrary invalid template code safe.

Candidate Formation and Immediate Context #

Overload resolution begins by forming candidates. For a function template, deduction or explicitly supplied arguments can require substitution into its function type and template parameter declarations. If that immediate declaration context is invalid, the specialization is discarded and another viable overload may be selected.

item.title: C++20 Concepts and Constraints
item.description:
C++20 concepts let a template declaration state compiler-checkable requirements at its interface. A constrained candidate participates in overload resolution only when its associated constraints are satisfied. Constraints therefore replace many std::enable_if SFINAE uses with declarations that expose the intended operation set; they do not prove the semantic requirements documented by an API.

item.title: C++ Language and Library Notes
item.description:
This bounded anthology collects language and toolchain-facing rules that do not require a separate article. Each section states the boundary that governs the feature, because similar-looking C++ spellings can have different ownership, lookup, or lifetime effects.

Resource Ownership and Optional State #

Ownership is the responsibility to release a resource at the correct time. Model it with RAII: acquire in construction, release in destruction, and make the object’s invariant hold across exceptional control flow. Prefer the Rule of Zero when members such as std::unique_ptr or std::vector already implement the resource policy. A type that directly manages a raw resource must define a coherent destructor, copy policy, move policy, and failure policy.

item.title: C++ Declarations, Definitions, and Linkage
item.description:
A declaration introduces a name and describes its type. A definition supplies the entity that the program uses. Linkage determines whether declarations in different scopes or translation units denote the same entity, while storage duration determines how long an object exists. Keeping those four questions separate makes dense C and C++ declarations easier to reason about.

Read a Declarator from Its Name #

item.title: C++ Template Specialization
item.description:
Specialization supplies a definition for a particular template argument list or, for class and variable templates, for a more specific argument pattern. Select specialization only when type-based dispatch is the appropriate interface; use ordinary overloads for function-specific dispatch and concepts for behavioral eligibility.

Full Specializations #

A full specialization names every argument and begins with template <>. Function, class, and variable templates can be fully specialized.

cpp 
template <class T>
struct formatter {
 static const char* name() { return "other"; }
};

template <>
struct formatter<int> {
 static const char* name() { return "int"; }
};

A full specialization is an independent entity. It does not inherit members, definitions, or default template arguments from the primary template; define everything it needs. Declare a full specialization before the first use that would otherwise implicitly instantiate that specialization in every translation unit that uses it.

item.title: C++ Implementation Idioms
item.description:
An implementation idiom should make an ownership, lifetime, or dependency boundary explicit. Concise syntax is useful only when the associated invalidation and complexity rules remain visible to the reader.

Erase-Remove for Sequence Containers #

std::remove and std::remove_if are algorithms; they rearrange a range so retained elements occupy a prefix and return the new logical end. They neither erase elements nor change a container’s size. Erase the suffix immediately when the container provides an erase range overload.

item.title: C++ Copy Elision and Return Values
item.description:
Copy elision permits an implementation to omit copy or move construction even when that constructor or destructor has observable side effects. Before C++17, every elision case was permitted but optional. C++17 changed prvalue semantics, making several former temporary-elision cases direct construction instead.

Returned Prvalues and Named Locals #

Since C++17, a prvalue of the function return type returned from a function constructs the result object directly. A deleted copy and move constructor therefore do not prevent this form, although the returned type’s destructor must still be accessible and non-deleted at the return statement:

item.title: C++ Random Number Facilities
item.description:
The C++ random library separates a deterministic engine from a distribution. An engine produces a sequence of uniformly distributed values over its specified output range. A distribution consumes engine output and maps it to a requested statistical distribution. Keep both objects alive when their state must continue.

cpp 
#include <random>

std::mt19937_64 engine{std::random_device{}()};
std::uniform_int_distribution<int> die{1, 6};

int roll = die(engine); // Both engine and distribution may advance state.

std::mt19937 and std::mt19937_64 are pseudo-random engines: a fixed initial state produces a reproducible sequence. std::default_random_engine is implementation-defined, so it is unsuitable when tests, files, or protocols require the same sequence across implementations.

item.title: C++ Classes and Special Member Functions
item.description:
A C++ class defines representation, invariants, and the operations that establish and preserve them. Constructors establish an object’s invariant, member functions preserve it, and the destructor releases resources owned by that object. Design the ownership policy first, because it determines whether compiler-generated special members are correct.

Construction and Destruction #

A constructor has the class name and no return type. A default constructor has no parameters or has defaults for all its parameters. Copy and move constructors initialize a new object from an lvalue or rvalue of the same class; copy and move assignment update an existing object.

item.title: C++ Exceptions and Exception Safety
item.description:
Exceptions separate reporting a failed operation from propagating it to a boundary that can respond. An exception transfers control to a matching handler; while control travels outward, C++ destroys every fully constructed automatic object whose scope is exited, in reverse construction order. Resource acquisition is initialization (RAII) therefore makes the normal and exceptional cleanup paths the same.

cpp 
void load_configuration(std::filesystem::path path) {
 std::ifstream input{path}; // Closed during unwinding.
 if (!input) {
 throw std::runtime_error{"cannot open configuration"};
 }
 // Parsing may throw; input still closes.
}

try {
 load_configuration("app.conf");
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
 report(error.what());
}

Throw exception objects by value and catch polymorphic exception types by const reference. Catching a base exception by value slices a derived object. A catch (...) belongs only at a boundary that can restore an invariant, translate an error, or deliberately terminate; it must not silently continue with damaged state.

item.title: C++ Smart Pointers and Ownership
item.description:
Smart pointers make ownership visible in an interface. They do not replace references and raw pointers used solely to borrow an object whose lifetime is guaranteed elsewhere. Select the pointer type from the lifetime contract, then make transfer and observation explicit at API boundaries.

Unique Ownership #

std::unique_ptr<T> owns one object and is move-only. Create it with std::make_unique when ordinary new and the default deleter are appropriate; pass or return it by value to transfer ownership.

item.title: C++ Static Initialization Order
item.description:
C++ assigns storage duration independently of scope. Initialization and destruction rules for static and thread storage determine whether an object is available before main, on first use, or once per thread.

Storage Duration and Initialization Phases #

Namespace-scope objects, static data members, and block-scope static objects have static storage duration. thread_local objects have thread storage duration: each thread has a distinct instance, initialized as that thread starts or first uses it according to the declaration and implementation rules.

item.title: C++ Language Rules and Named Requirements
item.description:
C++ language rules determine whether a program is well-formed and what its execution means. Library named requirements and concepts add contracts for generic code. Similar terminology can hide an important distinction: a compiler can check expressions and types, but it cannot prove every semantic, complexity, validity, or equality promise made by a type.

Definitions and the One-Definition Rule #

Every odr-used non-inline function or variable needs one definition in the program. Declarations can be repeated when compatible, which makes forward declarations possible.

item.title: The C and C++ Preprocessor
item.description:
The preprocessor transforms preprocessing tokens before the C or C++ parser sees declarations, types, namespaces, or overloads. It expands includes, evaluates conditional directives, and performs macro replacement. Treat its output as generated source code, because language-level scope and type checking cannot repair an unsafe expansion.

Include Search Is a Build-Tool Contract #

#include "project/header.hpp" and #include <library/header> identify header-name tokens, not filesystem paths prescribed by the language standard. The mapping from a header name to a source file, including quote-versus-angle search order, is implementation-defined. Toolchains commonly search the including file’s directory and quote-specific paths for quotes, while angle headers begin in configured system paths; consult the compiler’s documentation and the build command for the actual order.

item.title: C++ Design Guidelines
item.description:
C++ interfaces should encode ownership, lifetime, and substitutability in types and signatures. The C++ Core Guidelines’ Rule of Zero follows from this design: a domain value composed from RAII members should not manually reproduce their copying, moving, and destruction behavior.

Resource Owners and Domain Values #

A resource-owning type acquires one resource, releases it in its destructor, and states whether copying or transfer is permitted. A handle represents access to a resource; an owning handle also bears responsibility for release. It is appropriate when a standard owner does not represent the resource’s acquisition, release, or error policy:

item.title: Testing C and C++ Programs
item.description:
C and C++ tests are executable programs whose status must affect the build and CI result. A framework can improve assertions and reporting, but a test executable with a dedicated main and deterministic dependencies is sufficient when integrated with the project’s test runner.

Build Tests as First-Class Targets #

Compile test targets separately from production binaries and link them against the production library. Register every executable with the existing test runner, such as CTest, Meson, or Automake TESTS, so a nonzero exit status fails CI.

item.title: Variadic Programming in C and C++
item.description:
C++ variadic templates preserve the type and count of every argument. C ellipsis functions erase that information, which shifts type interpretation and argument-count discipline to the caller. Prefer C++ packs for new typed interfaces.

Packs, Expansions, and Folds #

A template parameter pack and a function parameter pack may contain zero or more elements. A pack expansion applies a pattern once per element.

cpp 
#include <utility>

template <class Function, class... Ts>
decltype(auto) invoke(Function&& function, Ts&&... values) {
 return std::forward<Function>(function)(std::forward<Ts>(values)...);
}

template <class... Ts>
auto sum(Ts... values) {
 return (0 + ... + values); // binary left fold; 0 is the empty-pack identity
}

std::forward preserves the value category deduced for each forwarding reference. It does not extend an argument’s lifetime, so a callee must still obey its ordinary reference and ownership contract.

item.title: C++ Initialization
item.description: Initialization gives an entity its first value or establishes a reference binding. Assignment changes an object that already exists. Because constructors participate only in initialization and assignment operators participate only after lifetime has begun, the distinction affects overload resolution, invariants, and performance.

item.title: Compiler Builtins and Bit Operations
item.description:
GCC and Clang provide builtin spellings for operations that their front ends recognize directly. Bit-counting builtins can lower to a target instruction, a library sequence, or an optimized expression depending on the selected target and optimization context. Source code should choose the interface that states its portability and zero-input contract.

item.title: C++ Ranges and Views
item.description:
The ranges library separates the ability to iterate from ownership, traversal strength, and lazy transformation. A range supplies iteration boundaries; a view is a range suited to adaptor pipelines; an adaptor builds a new view whose elements are evaluated when iteration requests them.

cpp 
#include <ranges>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> source{1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
auto even_squares = source
 | std::views::filter([](int value) { return value % 2 == 0; })
 | std::views::transform([](int value) { return value * value; });

Constructing even_squares does not transform every element. Iteration invokes the predicate and transformation, so changes to source before iteration can be observed subject to the source container’s invalidation rules.

item.title: GCC Driver and Toolchain
item.description:
gcc and g++ are GCC driver programs. They select a language front end from input suffixes and options, run preprocessing and compilation, invoke the assembler, and coordinate the linker. The GCC manual is authoritative because exact defaults depend on the configured target and GCC release.

Driver Stages and Language Defaults #

For a source file, the driver can stop after preprocessing (-E), compilation to assembly (-S), or assembly to an object (-c). Without a stopping option it links the resulting objects and libraries.

item.title: C++ Template Metaprogramming and Type Traits
item.description:
Template metaprogramming selects types and values during translation. The standard type-traits library supplies common building blocks; constexpr, if constexpr, and concepts express many decisions more directly than recursive class-template specializations.

Traits, Transforms, and Predicates #

Traits conventionally expose a nested type or a value. Standard aliases ending in _t extract a type, while variable templates ending in _v extract a Boolean or other value.

cpp 
#include <concepts>
#include <type_traits>

template <class T>
using storage_type = std::remove_cvref_t<T>;

template <class T>
inline constexpr bool is_plain_object_v =
 std::same_as<T, std::remove_cvref_t<T>>;

Use transforms to normalize interfaces deliberately:

item.title: C++ Template Fundamentals
item.description:
A template is a declaration family parameterized by types, constant values, templates, and packs. A specialization is formed under C++ name lookup, type checking, overload resolution, and constraint rules; templates are not textual substitution.

Template Parameters #

Type parameters accept types, constant template parameters accept structural constant values, and template template parameters accept a compatible template. Defaults provide omitted arguments. A parameter pack represents zero or more parameters or arguments.

item.title: Clang-Format
item.description:
clang-format makes source layout a repository policy rather than a per-author preference. It formats supported languages from a syntactic token stream, so indentation, wrapping, and many spacing decisions are reproducible. It does not establish naming, API, ownership, or behavioral correctness; review must still examine those semantic concerns.

Establishing Repository Policy #

Commit a .clang-format file at the repository root. With --style=file, clang-format searches from each input file toward its ancestor directories and selects the closest .clang-format or _clang-format. A nested directory can therefore deliberately override a root policy, but an accidental nested file changes the result for that subtree.

item.title: C++ Value Categories and Move Semantics
item.description:
Move semantics are overload selection and type-defined state transfer, not an automatic transfer of ownership. Begin with an expression’s value category, then choose a parameter type that describes ownership and lifetime.

Expression Categories #

Every non-void expression is exactly one of these categories:

  • An lvalue identifies an object, function, or bit-field.
  • An xvalue identifies an object whose resources may be reused.
  • A prvalue computes a value or initializes an object.

Lvalues and xvalues are glvalues; prvalues and xvalues are rvalues. A named variable is an lvalue expression even when it has type T&&.
